topic.title: Confidence & Self-Trust
topic.description: Help your child build real confidence from the inside out

articles.title: Redefining Confidence — Self-Trust, Not Feeling Good
articles.description: We picture a confident kid as a happy, bold one.
articles.content:
# Redefining Confidence — Self-Trust, Not Feeling Good

We picture a confident kid as a happy, bold one. But real confidence is quieter: a child who can feel disappointed, nervous, or left out — and still, underneath, feel like a good person. Not feeling good. Trusting themselves. That one shift changes how you respond to almost everything.

## Why This Works

A feeling can't be the enemy of confidence, because feelings arrive whether we invite them or not. So confidence isn't feeling good — it's the range of feelings a child can have while still feeling okay about who they are. A narrow range ("I'm only fine when I'm happy") is fragile. A wide one ("I can be jealous, scared, wrong — and still me") is durable. Every time we rush to argue a child out of a hard feeling, we quietly teach the opposite: some feelings make you unacceptable, so hurry up and stop having them. There's a second engine underneath. A child is always half-asking "who am I, and am I good?" — and they read the answer off us: what we notice out loud, what we name, and especially the labels we toss to other grown-ups over their heads all pile up into their picture of themselves.

## What To Do

- When a hard feeling shows up, sit down beside it instead of talking your child out of it. "You really wanted to win. That stings." — full stop, no rescue tacked on.
- Catch yourself fast-forwarding. One shy morning isn't a lifelong verdict; a rough week is weather, not climate. Name it as a moment, not a trend.
- Mind the labels you hand other adults while your child can hear — "he's my difficult one" lands harder than you think. They're listening for who they are.
- If your child hangs back at the edge of something new, read it as care, not cowardice — a child sizing up a room is trusting their own gut. (For the in-the-moment lines, see the shyness and slow-to-warm-up guide; this chapter is the bigger picture.)
- Aim at the widest range, not the narrowest. The goal isn't a child who only feels good — it's one who can feel anything and stay okay with themselves.
- Practice on yourself. Tuck a five-second check into something you already do — "How am I, really?" at the kettle — so self-trust is something you live, not just preach.

## What To Say

- "That's a big, hard feeling. You're allowed to have it. I'm not going anywhere."
- "You know yourself. If it felt unfair to you, then it felt unfair."
- To another grown-up, in front of your child: "She takes her time warming up — and she's wonderful once she does."
- To yourself, at the sink: "I'm allowed to find this hard. Nothing is wrong with me."

## Common Pitfalls

- Treating confidence as a mood to boost rather than a trust to build — pep talks fade; being accompanied sticks.
- "Cheering up" as a reflex, which tells a child their real feeling was the wrong answer.
- Deciding who a child *is* from their hardest ten minutes.
- Coaching self-trust in your child while trashing yourself out loud — they learn the version you model, not the one you recommend.

## When To Seek Support

Ordinary self-doubt comes and goes. But if your child's sense of being fundamentally bad or worthless is constant, heavy, and doesn't lift with steady warmth over weeks — or shows up as withdrawal, hopelessness, or not wanting to be here — that's beyond confidence-building. Talk with your pediatrician or a child mental-health professional. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: Naming Feelings, Not Fixing Them
articles.description: Putting a feeling into words does something bigger than calming it down.
articles.content:
# Naming Feelings, Not Fixing Them

Putting a feeling into words does something bigger than calming it down. It hands your child a vocabulary for their own insides — and the message that feelings are normal, nameable things, not problems to hurry past. This chapter is about naming and asking, not soothing and fixing.

## Why This Works

A child who can name what's happening inside them can eventually handle it; a child with no words for it just gets flooded. Naming a feeling out loud — "that looks like frustration" — is a gift even when your child shrugs it off, because you're not trying to make the feeling leave. You're building the dictionary. Reassurance does the opposite of what we hope: "don't worry, you're fine!" quietly says the feeling was a mistake, something to be talked out of. Curiosity says the feeling makes sense and I want to understand it. And there's a specific move that builds confidence more than plain comfort does: not just naming the feeling, but handing your child authority over it — you're the one who knows your own insides. That second layer, more than the first, is what tells a child their inner world can be trusted.

## What To Do

- Name it without fixing it: say what you see ("that's disappointment"), then stop. No "but," no silver lining chasing it down.
- Go one step further and ask. Don't wait for feelings to erupt — invite them: "What was the best part and the worst part of today?"
- Trade reassurance for curiosity. Swap "you'll be fine" for "tell me what happened — then what?" and repeat back what you heard so they can correct you.
- Hand them the authority. After you name a feeling, give it back: "You're the expert on you — did I get that right?"
- For a kid who hates feelings-talk head-on, come in sideways. Skip the sit-down; let it slip out over blocks, in the car, mid-snack, or wrapped in a little humor. Same job, softer door.
- Let a "no" to talking be okay. "We don't have to talk about it. I'm around if the words show up later."

## What To Say

- "Your face looks heavy. Want to tell me, or just have company for a minute?"
- "That sounds like it felt really unfair. You'd know — you were there."
- "Then what happened? … Huh. And how did that sit with you?"
- Sideways, mid-drive: "Random question — what's the most annoying thing that happened today?"

## Common Pitfalls

- Racing to the reassurance ("you're great, don't be sad!") — it ends the very conversation you wanted.
- Naming a feeling and then arguing it down in the same breath.
- Interrogating. Three gentle questions land; twenty feel like a spotlight.
- Forcing the direct conversation on a child who does better sideways — the resistance is information, not defiance.

## When To Seek Support

If your child has almost no words for feelings well past the age peers are starting to find them, or can't recognize emotions in themselves or others in a way that's affecting daily life, mention it to your pediatrician — it's worth a look, not a worry. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: Where Lasting Self-Worth Comes From
articles.description: Praise a child for being smart, and you've handed them something they have to keep proving.
articles.content:
# Where Lasting Self-Worth Comes From

Praise a child for being smart, and you've handed them something they have to keep proving. Notice how hard they worked, and you've handed them something they own. Lasting self-worth grows from the parts a child controls — effort, care, curiosity, sticking with it — not the parts they don't: grades, trophies, being called "gifted." This chapter shifts your praise from the prize to the process.

## Why This Works

Worth built on outcomes needs constant refilling. A trophy feels great — for about a day — and then a gap opens between the high of being praised and how the child feels on a plain Tuesday. The wider that gap, the more a child's steadiness depends on the next win, and the more anxious the wait between wins becomes. Worth built on effort doesn't drain the same way, because effort is always available — a child can try hard on a day nothing goes right. Even glowing labels backfire here. "You're so smart" sounds like a gift, but it's really a title to defend: now every hard problem threatens it, so the child plays it safe to keep it. Praise the process and the title disappears — nothing to protect means room to struggle, try the harder thing, and grow.

## What To Do

- Swap the trophy for the try. Instead of "you're so smart," ask "how did you figure that out?" You don't have to pretend the win didn't happen — just put the weight on the part they did.
- Praise verbs, not labels — worked, kept going, noticed, fixed it — the things they can do again tomorrow.
- Go easy on "smart," "gifted," "a natural," "the pretty one." Even the kind ones become cages a child performs to stay inside.
- When someone else hands your child a label ("what a genius!"), don't correct the grown-up — help your child hold it lightly later: "Grandpa called you a genius. What was that like to hear?" No right answer; you're teaching them to weigh a label, not swallow it.
- Use "not yet" instead of "can't" — it puts your child in the gap between not-yet-able and able, where learning lives, instead of at a dead end.
- Let your child catch you struggling on purpose — fumble something, say "ugh, tricky, let me try that again" — so mistakes look like a normal part of being a person here. (For coaching a specific hard task in the moment, see the frustration-tolerance guide; this chapter is why it matters for how they see themselves.)

## What To Say

- "You practiced that every day this week. THAT'S what I want you to notice about yourself."
- "How'd you think to try it that way?"
- "You didn't have it yet — and then you kept going until you did."
- When a compliment flies in: "People will call you all sorts of things. What counts is what you know about how hard you worked."

## Common Pitfalls

- Dropping praise entirely — the goal is to aim it better, not go cold on a real accomplishment.
- Banning "smart" so hard it becomes a Thing — just shift your weight to effort and let it be quiet.
- Praising effort you invented ("you worked so hard!" on something easy) — kids clock the fake and stop trusting the real.
- Fixing the label a relative used in front of everyone — you don't need to; the private follow-up does the work.

## When To Seek Support

If your child falls apart at any mistake, avoids anything they might not ace, or ties their whole worth to one grade or result in a way that doesn't ease with steady, process-focused support, check in with your pediatrician or a child therapist. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: Talking Back to the Inner Critic — Perfectionism and Self-Doubt
articles.description: Kids don't outgrow a harsh inner voice by being told it's wrong.
articles.content:
# Talking Back to the Inner Critic — Perfectionism and Self-Doubt

Kids don't outgrow a harsh inner voice by being told it's wrong. "You're not stupid!" just argues with the voice — and loses. The move that works is stranger and gentler: help your child give that voice a name and a shape, so it becomes one loud part of them instead of the whole truth. Then make sure a braver voice gets airtime too.

## Why This Works

You can't delete a feeling by force. Push a self-critical thought down and it gathers strength and pops back up bigger. Name it, though — "oh, that's the never-good-enough voice again" — and something loosens. The thought stops being the child and becomes a thing the child *has*: one part with an opinion, not the final word. That's the whole trick — not silencing the harsh voice, but shrinking it back to its actual size. And here's the part that surprises parents: the goal isn't to swap the harsh voice for a cheerful one. Both voices get to live in there. You're not evicting the critic — you're making sure the braver, "I've done hard stuff before" voice is just as easy to hear. Kids pick this up fastest not when we diagnose it in them, but when they watch us live with our own version first.

## What To Do

- Give the critic a shape. Let your child name the voice that says they're bad at everything — something a little silly is perfect ("the Grumble-Gremlin"). Named and cartoonish, it stops feeling like the truth.
- Introduce it on yourself first, on a calm day: "You know, I've got a voice that tells me I'll mess up. I call it my Backseat Grumbler. Want to hear what it said today?"
- Grow the other voice on purpose. Help your child find a braver line that's theirs — "this part's tough, and tough is a thing I've done" — so it's loaded before they need it.
- Make it clear both voices stay. You're not deleting the mean one; you're turning up the brave one so it isn't drowned out. Nobody's insides are only cheerful, and that's fine.
- Turn the hard moment into a heads-up game. Before something tricky, guess together: "When do you think the Grumbler pipes up — at the start, or the tricky middle?" Expected, it's far less scary than an ambush. (This is about spotting the voice; for guessing where the task itself gets hard, see the frustration-tolerance guide.)

## What To Say

- "Sounds like the never-enough voice is loud right now. What's it saying? … Okay. And what does your brave voice say back?"
- "That's a thought you're having — it isn't a fact about you."
- "My Grumbler told me to quit today. I said thanks, I've got this. It hates that."
- "Let's guess when the tricky voice shows up this time, so it can't sneak up on you."

## Common Pitfalls

- Arguing with the voice ("that's not TRUE, you're amazing!") — it digs in, and now your child is defending it.
- Trying to delete the critic instead of turning up the brave one — gone-for-good isn't the goal, and promising it backfires.
- Diagnosing the voice in your child before you've ever shown them yours.
- Naming it once and dropping it — this is a habit you build over weeks, not a one-time talk.

## When To Seek Support

A little self-criticism is normal. But if your child's harsh voice is relentless — constant "I'm worthless / everyone hates me / I ruin everything" that doesn't ease with steady support, or arrives with hopelessness or withdrawal — that's worth professional eyes. Talk to your pediatrician or a child therapist. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: The Kindest Believable Read, Turned Inward
articles.description: When your child stalls, stomps off, or "isn't even trying," you get to choose the story you tell about it — lazy and defiant, or stuck and overwhelmed.
articles.content:
# The Kindest Believable Read, Turned Inward

When your child stalls, stomps off, or "isn't even trying," you get to choose the story you tell about it — lazy and defiant, or stuck and overwhelmed. Both are guesses. But the generous guess keeps you warm, keeps them believing they're fundamentally good, and — over time — becomes the voice they learn to use on themselves. This chapter turns that generous read inward.

## Why This Works

Children build their self-image partly from the version of them we hand back. Reflect "you're being lazy" often enough and it becomes something a child quietly believes about who they are. Reflect "something's making this hard for you" and they get a different picture — a good person facing a problem, not a problem themselves. Neither read is certain; that's the point. You choose the kind one not because you've confirmed it's true, but because of what it grows. Underneath most "won't" sits a "can't-right-now" — a fear, an overwhelm, a harsh thought already running. Curiosity about that barrier gets you somewhere a lecture about effort never will. And the biggest payoff is delayed: a child met with generous reads for years slowly learns to give themselves one. The way we read them becomes the way they read themselves. (For the nuts and bolts of choosing that read in a live moment with your child, the cooperation guide covers it — this chapter is after the confidence payoff and how it turns inward.)

## What To Do

- Pick the generous guess out loud — and hold it as a guess. "I don't think you're giving up. I think something about this got hard." You're not claiming to know; you're choosing the read that helps.
- Treat "not trying" as a clue, not a verdict. Get curious about the barrier — "what's the tricky part?" — instead of turning up the pressure.
- Coach the inward version. When your child brands themselves ("I'm so dumb"), lend them the kinder read: "Or… you hit something hard and haven't cracked it yet. Try that version on."
- Narrate your own kind read of yourself where they can hear it. Mistakes and all, out loud, on ordinary days.
- Save the hardest generous read for yourself. When you snap, the story "I'm a terrible parent" helps no one — least of all your child, who needs you to recover, not spiral.

## What To Say

- "You're not lazy. Something's in the way. Let's find it together."
- "That's the harsh story. Here's a kinder one that might be just as true: this is hard, and you're not done yet."
- To yourself, after a rough moment: "I snapped. That's a thing I did — not the kind of parent I am. Repair, then move on."
- "I get things wrong sometimes and I'm still good at this. So are you."

## Common Pitfalls

- Stating your generous guess as a confirmed fact about their insides — hold it as the read you're choosing, not a diagnosis.
- Using the kind read to skip the repair — generosity isn't a pass on fixing what happened.
- Only ever aiming generosity outward — a parent who's brutal with themselves models the harsh voice, not the kind one.
- Turning "something's hard for you" into a reason to drop every expectation — it changes your tone, not your standards.

## When To Seek Support

If your child's self-talk stays relentlessly harsh no matter how consistently you offer a kinder read — or you can't find any generous read of your own child, and warmth feels gone for weeks — that's worth support, for them or for you. Talk to your pediatrician, a child therapist, or your own doctor. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: Body Confidence — Appearance, Self-Talk, and the Outside World
articles.description: A child's comfort in their own body doesn't come from being told they're cute.
articles.content:
# Body Confidence — Appearance, Self-Talk, and the Outside World

A child's comfort in their own body doesn't come from being told they're cute. It comes from feeling understood, in every mood — and, oddly, from a home that doesn't make a big deal of looks. The more appearance gets talked about, even kindly, the more a child learns it's the thing to track. This chapter takes the spotlight off looks and puts it on how a body feels and what it does.

## Why This Works

Praise about appearance, even the warmest kind, teaches a child that looks are the scoreboard — so they start checking it. A body feels like a good home to live in when a child has been met and understood across every feeling, not when they've been told they're good-looking. That's why "am I pretty?" is rarely really about pretty. Underneath it is a bigger question — am I okay, am I loved, am I enough — and answering the surface one ("yes, gorgeous!") leaves the real one untouched and teaches them to keep asking the mirror. What protects a child long-term isn't a parent who supplies better verdicts; it's one who hands the question back — how do *you* feel in it? — and who models questioning the appearance messages flying in from everywhere else.

## What To Do

- Answer the question under the question. When your child asks "am I pretty?", reach past the mirror: "You're wondering if you're okay just as you are. You are — completely. And how do you feel in that outfit?"
- Aim your comments at what a body does and how it feels — running, climbing, resting, hugging — not how it looks.
- In a raw moment — "I'm ugly," "I hate how I look" — do less, not more. Sit close, name the hurt ("that's a painful thing to feel about yourself"), and don't argue, fix, or analyze yet. The debate can wait; the comfort can't. Come back to it later, cooled off, with gentle curiosity — where the idea came from, how many people quietly feel it too.
- Model questioning out loud when an appearance message lands: "this ad says everyone should look one way — huh, is that true for everyone? at every age?" You don't need an answer; the pausing is the lesson.
- Keep your own harsh body talk out of earshot — kids absorb how you speak about your body as much as about theirs. Let them see you enjoy your body plainly instead: moving, resting, doing.
- If an outside grown-up — a relative, a coach, anyone — remarks on your child's size in front of them, calmly decline the framing right there ("we don't go by that — her body's doing exactly what it should"), then set the channel privately afterwards: anything about her body comes to you, not to her. What you say in the room outweighs what they said.

## What To Say

- "You're checking if you're alright exactly as you are. You are. Always."
- "I loved what your legs did on that climb today."
- "That feels awful to think about yourself. I'm right here — we don't have to solve it this second."
- "A kid at school said that? Let's wonder about it together — does that rule really work for everybody?"

## Common Pitfalls

- Answering "am I pretty?" with "yes, so pretty!" — it soothes for a second and teaches them to keep asking the mirror.
- Debating an "I'm ugly" in the hot moment — presence first; anything analytic much later, if at all.
- Swapping "you're beautiful" for "you're SO smart" — a different label is still a label to keep up.
- Forgetting your child hears you sigh at your own reflection.

## When To Seek Support

If your child fixates on their weight, size, or a body part, starts restricting, hiding, or overthinking food, or a negative body thought turns constant and heavy, don't handle it alone and don't turn it into a diet — loop in your pediatrician, who can look at eating, growth, and mood together. See the red-flags card.

scripts.title: A Relative Praises Your Child's Looks or Brains — To Their Face
scripts.scenario: At a family lunch, an aunt keeps telling your child, right to their face, how gorgeous and clever they are. Kindly meant — but you can feel it landing as pressure. You don't want to correct your aunt, and you don't want the label to stick.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
In the moment, light, no correction of the adult: "She's got a lot of opinions about you — lucky you!" and move on.

Later, one-on-one: "Auntie called you smart and pretty a bunch today. What was that like to hear? … No wrong answer — I'm just curious."

If they liked it: "Makes sense, it feels nice. And you're so much more than either of those."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Don't contradict the other adult in front of your child — it makes a scene and teaches nothing
- Later, hand the label back to your child to weigh, without supplying the verdict yourself
- Aim your own follow-up praise at what they control — how kind, how curious, how hard they try

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: This is a repeatable move, not a one-off. Over time your child learns to treat any label — flattering or not — as an outside opinion to notice, not a fact to swallow.

scripts.title: "I Can't Do Anything Right" in the Middle of Something Hard
scripts.scenario: Your child is mid-way through building a marble run that keeps collapsing, and out it comes: "I can't do anything right. I'm the worst." They're not lazy and not really quitting — they're stuck and flooded.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
First, the kind read, out loud: "You're not bad at this. You hit a hard part and it's getting to you."

Name the voice: "Sounds like that never-good-enough voice got loud. What's it saying?"

Then the braver one: "Okay — what could your other voice say back? … 'This part's tough, and I've done tough before.' Want to borrow that one?"

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Read the meltdown as an unnamed hard feeling, not laziness — respond with curiosity, not a pep talk or a consequence
- Separate the thought from the child: it's a voice they're hearing, not the truth about them
- Stay near and let them try the next small piece with you, no takeover

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Later, calm, plant the heads-up: "Next time we build, let's guess when the never-enough voice shows up — so it can't ambush you." For coaching the task itself in the moment, see the frustration-tolerance guide.

scripts.title: When a Half-Finished Project Gets Crumpled in Frustration
scripts.scenario: Your child was shaping a clay dog. The legs keep flopping, and suddenly they squash the whole thing flat: "It's stupid. I'm done." The tears are right behind it.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Meet the feeling, not the clay: "Ohh. It wasn't turning out the way you pictured, and that is so frustrating."

Give the urge a shape: "That squash-it-all feeling — that's the 'if it's not perfect it's ruined' voice. I get that one too."

Offer the door back: "The dog can rest. When you're ready, we can fix one leg — just one — together. Or start fresh. Your call."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Don't rescue the object or scold the squashing — go to the disappointment underneath it
- Name the perfectionistic urge as a part, so it isn't the whole child
- Leave the choice to re-enter with them; forced continuation feeds the voice

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: On a calm day, model your own version: fumble something small on purpose, say "not perfect — still good enough," and let them watch you keep going.

scripts.title: "Do I Look Good?" — The Everyday Mirror Question
scripts.scenario: Getting dressed for the day, your child spins around: "Do I look pretty? Does this look good on me?" No crisis — just an offhand ask, eyes on you for the verdict.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Hand the question back: "Ooh — how does it feel to YOU? Comfy? Fun to move in? That's the part that counts."

Answer the bigger question underneath: "And if you're asking whether you're great exactly as you are — you are, dressed any which way."

Skip the rating: not "yes, gorgeous!" but "you look like you, and I love that."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Treat the looks question as a stand-in for "am I okay?" and answer that one warmly
- Redirect to how the outfit feels and what they like, not your external score
- Keep your own comments aimed at function and feeling over appearance

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: If the mirror-checking turns frequent or anxious, notice what else is going on that week — the question often spikes when something unrelated has them feeling wobbly.

scripts.title: Catching "You're So Smart!" Before It Leaves Your Mouth
scripts.scenario: Your child solves a puzzle fast and looks up, glowing. "You're so smart!" is halfway out of your mouth — and you remember you wanted to praise differently, without going cold on a real win.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Swap the label for the process, warmth intact: "Whoa — how did you figure that out so fast? Show me your thinking!"

Name the doing, not the trait: "You tried three ways and stuck with it till it clicked. THAT'S the good stuff."

You can still cheer the win — just aim it: "That was hard and you got it, because you kept at it."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Keep the warmth; only move the weight from "who you are" to "what you did"
- Praise verbs they can repeat tomorrow — tried, stuck with it, noticed, fixed
- Don't fake effort praise on something easy; find the real doing to name

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: No need to ban "smart." Just let effort get the spotlight most days, and watch your child start narrating their own effort back to you.

scripts.title: Your Child Overhears You Criticize Your Own Body
scripts.scenario: Yanking at your shirt in the mirror, you mutter "ugh, I look awful in this." A small voice behind you: "Mama, do you not like your body?" You didn't know they were there.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Don't wave it off — repair plainly: "You heard me being unkind about my own body. That wasn't fair — to me, or to your ears."

Model the reset: "My body carried groceries and gave good hugs today. It's a good body. I'm going to talk to it nicer."

Return to them, no appearance verdict: "And your body is yours and good, full stop."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Name it and course-correct rather than pretending they didn't hear
- Show the repair out loud — kids learn as much from the fix as they'd have absorbed from the slip
- Move your hard body-talk out of earshot going forward — process it with another grown-up

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Let your child regularly see you enjoy your body plainly — moving, resting, doing — not evaluating it. That's the quiet lesson that outlasts any single slip.

scripts.title: A Doctor or Coach Comments on Your Child's Size — In Front of Them
scripts.scenario: At a checkup, the doctor says, right in front of your seven-year-old, that they should "watch the weight." You see your child's face fall. You have about two seconds.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Calm, in the room, declining the framing: "We keep body-size talk out of the room with her — her body's doing exactly what it should. If there's something medical, let's you and I talk separately."

To your child, warmly: "Your body is good and strong. That's grown-up stuff for me to sort out, not yours to carry."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Your calm counter-statement in the room matters more to your child than the original comment
- Afterwards, set the channel once and plainly — with the practice, the coach, the relative: anything about her body or weight comes to us adults directly, not to her
- Take any real medical concern about eating, growth, or weight to the pediatrician privately — never make it your child's problem or a diet

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: For an older child, debrief gently later: "That felt yucky when the doctor said it, huh. I didn't love it either. You just get to like your body — the numbers are for me and the doctor to sort out." If eating or growth is a genuine worry, that is a private, professional conversation.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Route any concern about eating, growth, or weight to your pediatrician privately; never restrict a child's food without medical guidance.

scripts.title: Your Child Loudly Points Out a Stranger's Body in Public
scripts.scenario: On the city bus, your child asks at full volume, pointing: "Why is that lady in a wheelchair?" Three rows hear it. Your face goes hot.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Plain and unhurried — no shushing, no speech: "She uses a wheelchair to get around. Lots of people do."

Then turn the person back into a person: "Want to say hi when we go past?"

If your child keeps drilling, park it warmly: "Great question. Let's talk about it properly at home — I'll tell you everything I know."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Answer the actual question in one calm sentence — a hot "shhh!" teaches that bodies are shameful to mention
- Shift from observing to greeting where it fits; a wave treats the person as someone to meet, not something to explain
- Save the full curiosity conversation for home, and actually have it

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: At home, open it back up: "You asked about the lady on the bus. What did you want to know?" Answer plainly. Then the house rule, in both directions: "Bodies aren't for public comments — other people's or yours. Questions always come to me, any time."

scripts.title: The Same Harsh Phrase, Task After Task
scripts.scenario: It's not just one bad moment anymore. "I'm so stupid," "I always mess up," "I ruin everything" — you're hearing it across homework, drawing, getting dressed, most days this month.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Name the pattern kindly: "I keep hearing that voice call you stupid. It's around a lot lately, huh."

Separate voice from child: "That's a voice you're hearing — it is not the truth about you, even when it's loud."

Grow the counter-voice on purpose, daily: "Let's catch one thing your brave voice can say, and practice it when things are calm — not only when it's hard."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Work the naming technique consistently — a harsh voice this frequent needs repetition, not one talk
- Look for patterns: a certain subject, time of day, or pressure that reliably sets it off
- Keep offering the kinder read even when it doesn't seem to land yet

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Some self-criticism is normal; this much, this often, is worth watching. If the harshness stays constant for weeks despite steady support, or comes with sadness, withdrawal, or "I wish I wasn't here," don't wait it out alone — check in with your pediatrician or a child therapist.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: If self-critical talk includes hopelessness or any wish not to exist, seek professional support promptly.

scripts.title: After You Snap: Getting Past Your Own Guilt
scripts.scenario: You lost it — sharper than you meant — over something small. Now your child is fine and playing, and you're stuck replaying it, sliding toward "I'm a terrible parent."

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
To yourself, the kinder-but-honest read: "I snapped. That's a thing I did — not the kind of parent I am. I can own it and repair it."

Out loud to your child, the repair: "I used a big sharp voice earlier, and that wasn't about you. I'm sorry. I'm working on it."

Not the spiral, not the excuse — just: "Missed that one. Repair, reset, keep going."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Give yourself the same generous read you'd give your child — harsh self-judgment models the harsh voice
- Separate the action ("I snapped") from your identity ("I'm bad at this") — one you can fix, the other just sinks you
- Repair simply and specifically; don't over-apologize or make your child comfort you

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Self-kindness here isn't letting yourself off the hook — it's what frees up the energy to actually change the pattern. A parent who can recover models the exact resilience you want for your child.
